title: Patton crosses the Moselle

facts.text: On 14 November 1944, Lt. Gen. George S. Patton went across the Moselle to see the bridgehead his 90th Infantry Division had won at Koenigsmacker, north of Metz.

With him were Maj. Gen. Walton Walker of XX Corps and Brig. Gen. James Van Fleet, commander of the 90th Division. They rode in an armored car to the division's command post, then toured the freed town in jeeps.
Five days earlier, early on 9 November, the 90th had crossed the Moselle in assault boats at the height of a flood.
Opposite Fort Koenigsmacker the river was almost a mile wide and in places four feet deep, spilling into the villages on its west bank.
The first battalion pushed off at 3:30 a.m., and another followed in four waves of 40 assault boats each.
Fort Koenigsmacker, built by the Germans between 1908 and 1915, had four 100 mm guns in revolving armored turrets, and its fire wrecked bridging equipment and harried the men in the boats.
Engineers blasting their way into the fort used so much explosive that more had to be dropped in by air. The garrison gave up on 11 or 12 November; accounts differ.
Taking the fort cost about 111 American casualties, and more than 300 Germans were killed, wounded, or captured.
On the night of 11 to 12 November, the 25th Panzergrenadier Division counterattacked at Kerling with about ten tanks and assault guns. The attack failed.
The water ran so high and fast that five days passed before armor could cross the Moselle there in force.
Patton called it 'an epic river crossing.'
The bridgehead was the northern arm of a pincer. Third Army closed the ring around Metz on 19 November, and fighting in the city ended on 22 November.

photoNote: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton, in helmet and trench coat, talks with Maj. Gen. Horace McBride of the 80th Infantry Division at its command post, Ville au Val, Lorraine, 3 November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo 111-SC-196153 (photographer Mastrosimone), NARA, public domain, full size 2416 px. Eleven days before the Koenigsmacker visit and not the 90th Division; the caption should say Patton in Lorraine that month. Same trench coat as in the 14 November film.
photoCredit: Lt. Gen. George S. Patton at the 80th Infantry Division command post in Lorraine, 3 November 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, NARA 111-SC-196153, public domain.

declassified.fact: The fort's defenders were not the only Germans caught. On 11 November a German relief patrol of 145 men, sent to help the garrison, walked into an American ambush and was captured.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Army Signal Corps film, story LIB 639 'Generals at Front, Koenigsmacher', 14 Nov 44 on the shot card, with a cameraman's slate in the film (166th Signal Photo Co., Sgt. Marder, 'Gen Patton with ... visit 90th Div', 11/14/44). Silent. The file is the stretch from 5:32 to 7:44 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times (checked on a contact sheet): 0:04 to 0:15 Patton, Walker, and Van Fleet outside a building; 0:20 to 0:30 close shots of Patton in his trench coat; 0:36 Patton climbs into the armored car; about 0:55 to 1:05 the armored car drives through the muddy street, the best moving opener; 1:08 the slate; 1:16 to 2:05 the generals and jeeps in the freed town. The reel's earlier stories (102nd Division, Compiegne Armistice Day) are left out.

This is real U.S. Army Signal Corps film shot on 14 November 1944: Patton with Maj. Gen. Walton Walker and Brig. Gen. James Van Fleet, the armored car in the muddy street, and jeeps in the freed town. The original film is silent.
